The effects of micro-aeration on semi-continued anaerobic digestion
of corn straw with increasing organic loading rates

a b s t r a c t
The beneﬁts of micro-aeration on batch anaerobic digestion (AD) of organic wastes have been intensively
studied. However, the effects of micro-aeration on the semi-continued AD under different organic
loading rates (OLRs) were still lacking. This study investigated the effects of micro-aeration on semi-
continued AD of corn straw with increasing OLRs from 1.1 to 2.1 volatile solid (VS)/(L$day). Results
showed micro-aeration could beneﬁt the AD process by increasing the median daily methane yields for
6%, 10% and 8% at OLRs of 1.1, 1.5 and 2.1 VS/(L$day), respectively. Moreover, micro-aeration stimulated
the growth of facultative bacteria (Clostridia), which secreted more critical enzymes (e.g., cellulase and
xylanase) and led faster degradation of corn straw as well as higher soluble humic acids (SHAs) con-
centration. The SHAs might act as electron shuttle to facilitate the direct interspecies electron transfer
(DIET)
among
syntrophic
bacteria
(Cloacimonadia)
and
hydrogenotrophic
methanogens
(Meth-
anobacterium), which led to a faster volatile fatty acids (VFAs) conversion into methane. This study
conﬁrmed the beneﬁcial effects of micro-aeration on the semi-continued AD at different OLRs and
unraveled the mechanisms behind.

1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a vivid technology in renewable
energy production, waste streams stabilization, and greenhouse
emissions reduction [1]. However, the applications of AD technol-
ogy often meet many barriers such as long fermentation time, low
substrate conversion efﬁciencies, and vulnerability to the impacts
of toxic or high organic loading rate (OLR) [2e4]. The reason for the
barriers mentioned above could be explained by the inherent dif-
ﬁculty in maintaining a metabolism balance among series of
microorganisms (i.e., hydrolytic bacteria, acidogens, acetogens, and
methanogens) [5]. Moreover, the interactions between these mi-
crobial communities are still poorly unraveled [6]. Managing or
altering the microbial community compositions to achieve speciﬁc
goals that is the so-called microbial resource management has been
considered as an efﬁcient way to inﬂuence the outcome of the AD
process [7]. Microbial resource management has been also proved
to be efﬁcient in increasing the tolerance of AD system to ammonia
[8], lipid-rich substrate [9], as well as in enhancement of the
lignocellulosic materials biodegradation [10,11], etc.
Oxygen is traditionally considered as an inhibiting factor for AD
process [5]. However, recent studies have proved a little breath of
oxygen or air introduced into the AD process (that is so called
micro-aeration) could beneﬁt the AD performance by regulation
the microbial community composition [5,12,13]. For example, Fu
et al. [12], found that micro-aeration at the intensity of 12.5 ml air/
Lreactor per day led 16.5% higher methane yield from AD of corn
straw. The methanogenesis and hydrolysis efﬁciency of blackwater

increased from 39.6% to 50.7% and from 34.7% to 48.7%, respectively
[14]. The total VFAs concentration rapidly decreased and its inhi-
bition effect on methanogens was alleviated when ORP-controlled
micro-aeration was adopted during AD of Napier grass at high
organic loading rate [5]. As reported in previous studies, micro-
aeration could stimulate growth of facultative bacteria, which
would produce more extracellular enzyme in turn, and promote
hydrolysis rate as well as VFAs production [12,15,16]. Nevertheless,
these studies were mainly conducted in batch experiment and low
organic loading rates. The effects of micro-aeration on semi-
continued AD of cellulosic substrate are rarely reported, the
mechanisms behind are also not fully revealed though it is vital to
AD process.
The aim of this study was to develop and validate the beneﬁcial
effects of micro-aeration on the semi-continued AD of corn straw
under increasing OLRs from 1.1 to 2.1 g VS/(L day). The mechanisms
behind were comprehensively analyzed according the reactor
performance, bacterial and archaeal community, extracellular
enzyme, and VFAs consumption etc. The implement of this study
could further deepen the understanding of micro-aeration and
provide references for its industrial application.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
Corn straw, a typical biomass waste in agriculture, was selected
as a representative lignocellulosic substrate in this paper. The
biomass was harvested from a corn farm (Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province,
China). The freshly corn straw was air-dried to the moisture content
about 6.6%, and then milled by a cutting mill (BJ-150, Baijjie,
Shanghai, China) to approximate particle size of 0.1 cm, which was
then stored in plastic vacuum bags for further use. The total solids
(TS), volatile solids (VS), content of hemicellulose, cellulose and
lignin of the corn straw were 93.4 ± 0.2%, 90.7 ± 0.2% (% of TS),
19.5 ± 4.6% (% of TS), 34.0 ± 2.0% (% of TS) and 22.7% ± 0.7% (% of TS),
respectively.
The inoculum used was granular anaerobic sludge that collected
from a mesophilic up-ﬂow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactor
treating citric acid wastewater. Before usage, the inoculum was
homogenize using a grinder (MJ-BL25B3, Midea, Guangdong,
China) for 3 min to obtain homogeneous liquid. The TS and VS of
the inoculum were 36.4 ± 3.7% and 34.6 ± 1.3% (% of TS).
2.2. Anaerobic reactor set-up and operation
The design of anaerobic reactor was shown in Fig. S1. Duplicate
semi-continued AD experiments were carried out in double-layer
glass reactors with working volume of 2 L. The hydraulic reten-
tion time (HRT) of reactors was set as 33 days, and the reactors were
running at 37 ± 1 C with water bath (HHeS24s, Dadi, Jintan, China)
heat preservation. The biogas produced was collected using 4 L gas
sampling bags (MBT32-4, Hedetech, Jiangsu, China). The organic
loading rates (OLRs) were increased gradually from 1.1 g VS/(L$day)
at the 1e118 days to 1.5 g VS/(L$day) at the 119e178 days, and
ﬁnally reached 2.1 g VS/(L$day) at the 179e238 days. The micro-
aeration intensity was set as 0.2 mL/(g$VS) according to our pre-
vious study [13], which was realized by pure oxygen (>99.98%)
injection from the bottom tube using a micro-peristaltic pump
(BT100-1L, LongerPump, Heibei, China) at the speed of 3.75 mL/h.
Based on the time of micro-aeration and OLRs, the two groups were
divided into 4 stages: Stage1, 1e50 days with the OLRs of 1.1 g VS/
(L$day) named C0 (without micro-aeration) and M0 (without
micro-aeration); Stage 2, 51e118 days with the OLRs of 1.1 g VS/
(L$day) named C1.1 (without micro-aeration) and M1.1 (micro-
aeration); Stage3, 119e178 days with the OLRs of 1.5 g VS/(L$day)
named C1.5 (without micro-aeration) and M1.5 (micro-aeration);
Stage 4,179e238 days with the OLRs of 2.1 g VS/(L$day) named C2.1
(without micro-aeration) and M2.1 (micro-aeration). For the start-
up of AD, nutrient solution [17] was used to adjust the working
volume to 2 L in each reactor, and the water discharged with
digestate was reﬁlled with tap water.
2.3. Effects of different concentrations of extracted SHAs on
methanogenesis
Effects of different concentrations of extracted SHAs on meth-
anogensis were explored in batch model using 4 g/L sodium acetate
as the sole substrate. Concentrations of SHAs were set as 0 (control),
0.5(SHAs0.5), 1 (SHAs1), and 2 (SHAs2) g/L, respectively. 60 mL
inoculum from the long-time running reactors was collected at the
220th day, which was then mixed with nutrient solution [17] to the
total liquid volume of 200 mL. Syringe bottles were purged with
nitrogen for 5 min to create anaerobic condition, sealed with rubber
stoppers and then incubated in a 37 C air bath at 200 rpm. The
biogas was measured in volume and composition every day. The
modiﬁed Gompertz model [18] was also used to ﬁt the cumulative
methane yield to analyze the effect of HAs concentration on the
methane productions (Supplementary InformationeSupporting
Methods).
2.4. Microbial community structure analysis
At the 118th, 178th and 238th day of AD, 10 mL of biogas slurry
were collected from control and micro-aeration reactors for mi-
crobial community structure analysis as the method described in
our previous study [19]. Brieﬂy, DNA was ﬁrstly extracted from
collected samples, and then the high throughput sequencing
method was used to analyze the microbial community structure.
The primer set for the V3eV4 region ampliﬁcation of the bacterial
16S rRNA gene was 338F (ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG) and 806R
(GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT), while the primer set for the V4eV5
region ampliﬁcation archaeal 16S rRNA gene was 524F (TGY-
CAGCCGCCGCGGTAA) and 958R (YCCGGCGTTGAVTCCAATT). The
gene data was processed on Illumina Miseq sequencing platform
(Majorbio, Shanghai, China) for the microbial diversity analysis. In
order to investigate the effects of micro-aeration on the extracel-
lular enzymes during AD process, PICRUSt, a software for the pre-
diction of genome functions, was used to predict the abundances of
hydrolytic enzymes by the online platform (Majorbio, Shanghai,
China) as described in a previous study [20].
2.5. Analytical methods
2.5.1. Analysis of soluble humic acids in digestate
Digestate for SHAs analysis were collected at 118th (C1.1 and
M1.1), 178th (C1.5 and M1.5) and 238th (C2.1 and M2.1) days. EEM
ﬂuorescence spectra was conducted to investigate the effects of
micro-aeration on SHAs in the collected digestate during the semi-
continued AD (Supplementary InformationeSupporting Methods).
In order to study the effects of micro-aeration on the concentration
of SHAs, SHAs were extracted according to the procedure devel-
oped by the International Humic Substances Society (IHSS), and the
gravimetric quantiﬁcation of the SHAs in g/L were conducted ac-
cording
to
the
details
in
the
Supplementary
Information-
Supporting Methods. The surface functional groups of SHAs pre-
cipitates were also analyzed through Fourier transform infrared
(FTIR) spectroscopy (IRTracer-100, Shimadzu, Japan).

2.5.2. Cyclic voltammetry (CV)
CV is a useful electrochemical method to analyze the redox
properties of materials and bio-system [21]. In order to study the
effects of micro-aeration on the redox properties of AD process,
digestate collected from control and micro-aeration reactors at the
end of experiment (238th day) were tested by a three electrode
electrochemical cell in a single chamber (Supplementary Infor-
mation -Supporting Methods).
The effects of extracted HAs on CV of digestate were also con-
ducted as follows: four solutions were prepared: 200 mL nutrient
solution [17], 200 mL nutrient solution þ0.2 g extracted SHAs,
100 mL nutrient solution þ 100 mL digestate, and 100 mL nutrient
solution þ 100 mL digestate þ 0.2 g extracted SHAs, namely,
Nutrient,
Nutrient
þ
SHAs,
Nutrient
þ
Digestate,
and
Nutrient þ Digestate þ SHAs, respectively.
2.5.3. Other analysis
The volume and composition of biogas, pH and VFAs concen-
tration were determined as the procedures described in our pre-
vious study [13].The TS and VS were determined according to the
gravimetric method [22]. Lignocellulosic compositions of corn
straw were analyzed according to the procedure developed by
National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) [23].
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Methane production from semi-continued anaerobic digestion
corn straw
Fig. 1a shows the daily methane yields during the AD of corn
straw under different OLRs in control and micro-aeration reactors.
The control and micro-aeration group possessed the same trend.
The daily methane yields in control and micro-aeration groups
were unstable until 50 days after start-up, then the reactors
reached a relatively stable status. When oxygen was beginning to
be injected into the micro-aeration reactors at 50th of AD, the daily
methane yield of the micro-aeration group was ﬁrstly negatively
affected by oxygen injection, and showed lower methane yield than
control from 51st to 77th d. Afterwards, the daily methane yield in
micro-aeration group was higher than control until the end of
experiment. The results indicated that the suddenly addition of
oxygen might interrupt the methane fermentation process and the
microorganisms in reactors could accommodate the micro-aeration
circumstances rapidly, which reﬂected as the increased methane
production.
In order to further analyzing the effect of micro-aeration on the
AD of corn straw under different OLRs, the daily methane yields
during the ﬁnal 30 days (when the reactors were running stably) of
each period were selected to represent the daily methane yield
variations and analyzed by violin with box plots, as shown in Fig.1b.
The black box and line whisker in both control and micro-aeration
groups became shorter with the increase of operation time, but the
median methane yields in two group were different. The median
daily methane yields in C0 and M0 were 231.7 ± 15.1 and
232.4 ± 10.2 NmL/(g$VS$d), indicating the successful start-up of the
control and micro-aeration groups. The median daily methane
yields in M1.1, M1.5 and M2.1 were 213.5 ± 9.4, 164.8 ± 5.5 and
152.9 ± 2.8 NmL/(g$VS$d), which were 6%, 10% and 8% higher than
those in C1.1, C1.5 and C2.1, respectively. Due to the complex
components and recalcitrant structure in lignocellulosic biomass,
the hydrolysis was considered as the rate-limiting process for AD
[5,13]. Micro-aeration has been reported to promote methane yield
by accelerating hydrolysis of AD in several studies [12,15,16]. The
results
demonstrated
that
micro-aeration
could
lead
higher
methane yields at semi-continued AD reactors with different
organic loads.

3.2. VFAs concentration variations under different OLRs in control
and micro-aeration reactors
In order to investigate the effects of micro-aeration on VFAs
productions during AD of corn straw under different OLRs, VFAs
concentrations in digestate were tested when the reactors were
running stably. The VFAs concentration variations under different
OLRs in control and micro-aerobic reactors are shown in Fig. 2.
During the experiment, acetate and propionate were the main
compositions of VFAs, while the concentrations of other volatile
fatty acids (e.g., butyrate) below the detectable limit. Similar results
were also reported that VFAs were only composited by acetate
(0.15 ± 0.22 g/L) and propionate (0.15 ± 0.25 g/L) during the semi-
continued AD of Napier grass at the OLR of 1.5 g VS/(L$day) [5]. VFAs
concentrations increased along with the increasing of OLRs. For
instance, at the ﬁnal day of each OLRs, total VFAs concentrations in
C1.1(118th d), C1.5(177th d) and C2.1 (238th d) were 0.41 ± 0.02,
0.53 ± 0.15 and 0.67 ± 0.18 g/L, respectively. Relatively, the total
VFAs concentrations in M1.1 (118th d), M1.5 (178th d) and M2.1
(238th d) were 0.49 ± 0.02, 0.65 ± 0.31 and 0.91 ± 0.30 g/L, which
were 20.0%, 45.7% and 35.2% higher than those in C1.1, C1.5 and C2.1,
respectively. The results reﬂected micro-aeration could enhance
the hydrolysis process of corn straw, which led increased VFAs
concentration.
3.3. Soluble humic acids released under different organic load rates
Lignocellulosic biomass like corn straw is composed by cellu-
lose, hemicellulose and lignin according non-covalent forces and
covalent cross-linkage [24]. Limited by the dense structure, hy-
drolysis step is considered as the rate-limiting step during AD of
corn straw [12]. To examine whether micro-aeration treatment
caused faster degradation of corn straw, EEM technique was
applied to analyze the biogas slurry obtained from different OLRs in
control and micro-aeration groups, which are shown in Fig. 3.
Fluorescence responses were weak in Regions I, II, III, and IV, while
the ﬂuorescence responses in Region V (represented humic acid-
like organics) were strong. Furthermore, ﬂuorescence responses
in Region V became stronger with micro-aeration and the increase
of OLRs. Consistent with the EEM results, the SHAs concentrations
in M1.1, M1.5 and M2.1 were 1.6 ± 0.1, 1.8 ± 0.1 and 2.1 ± 0.1 g/L,
which were 60.0%, 38.5% and 50.0% higher than those in C1.1, C1.5
and C2.1, respectively (shown in Fig. 4). As one of the by-products
during AD of cellulosic substrate, HAs are originated from the
degradation of lignin, cellulose and other non-lignin substances
through the metabolism of microorganisms [25]. Thus, higher
degradation of corn straw might lead increased concentration of
SHAs, which led to stronger ﬂuorescence response in Region V in
turn. The high degradation of corn straw could be further proved by
the methane yield as shown in Table 1. The average daily methane
yields from the ﬁnal 30 days in C1.1, M1.1, C1.5, M1.5, C2.1 and M2.1
were 441.5 ± 26.7, 468.0 ± 20.7, 470.9 ± 20.0, 517.8 ± 17.6,
629.6 ± 22.4 and 674.5 ± 22.7 NmL/d, which showed increasing
tendency with the micro-aeration and increased OLRs. The Max and
Min daily methane yield from the ﬁnal 30 days in C1.1, M1.1, C1.5,
M1.5, C2.1 and M2.1 shared the same trends with average methane
yields. Higher methane yield in micro-aeration and higher OLRs
groups reﬂected that more substances (corn straw) were converted
into methane, SHAs and other end-products by microorganisms in
anaerobic digesters.
3.4. Cyclic voltammetry analysis of digestats and the digestate with
HAs addition
AD is a process including a series of interdependent biochemical
steps carried out by diverse microorganisms (i.e., hydrolytic bac-
teria, acidogens, acetogens, and methanogens), in which metabolic
products like organics, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, electrons that
excreted by one group microbes are essential substrates for next
group of microbes [15]. Electrons ﬂows among microorganisms are
vital for the improvement of methane production and stabilization
of AD process [21], and the electron transfer capacity can be
analyzed by cyclic voltammetry method [26]. Fig. 5a shows the CV
at the scan rate of 50 mV/s of digestate from C2.1 and M2.1. It could
be observed that three distinct redox peaks with potentials of 0.68
(peak1), 0.28 (peak2), and 0.16 V (peak3) (versus saturated
calomel electrode) presented in all two groups. The peak1 currents
of M2.1 was 6.8 mA, which was 28.3% higher than that of C2.1, while
peak2 and peak3 currents showed little differences between C2.1
and M2.1. The higher peak currents occurred in M2.1 demonstrated
the higher capacity of electron transfer, which might attribute to
the increased SHAs under micro-aeration condition. And the result
was further conﬁrmed by Fig. 5b, which showed that the addition of
HAs promoted the peak currents in peak1 and peak2. As reported,
the HAs could act as electron transport medium [27e29] and the
higher SHAs concentration might lead higher electron transfer ca-
pacity to AD system, which reﬂected by the CV analysis. In addition,
FTIR analysis in Fig. S2 showed that the SHAs extracted from
digestate of AD of corn straw contained abundance of surface
oxygen-containing functional groups like CeO, C]O, and CeO,
which could serve as electron transport medium and led higher
electron transfer capacity to AD system [21]. The results indicated
that micro-aeration might create a favorable electron transfer
environment for the metabolisms of syntrophic microorganisms.
3.5. Analysis of the microbial community structure
The bacterial community structures at class level are shown in
Fig. 6a. The relative abundances of Clostridia in M1.1, M1.5 and M2.1
were 13.0%,17.8% and 23.3%, which were 16%, 9.4% and 13.9% higher
than those of C1.1, C1.5, and C2.1, respectively. Clostridia (phylum
Firmucutes) are well known to play a vital role in the AD of organic
waste for their ability to excrete extracellular enzyme to accelerate

M2.1 at the class level, which were 13.0% and 24.0% after running

obligatory syntrophism with other microorganisms [31]. In this
study, the relative abundance of Cloacimonadia increased obviously
after a long-time cultivation, which could be further increased
under micro-aeration condition. Similar results were proved by a
recent study that the relative abundance of Cloacimonadia under
sustainable supply of nano-oxygen bubbles increased from 1.8% to
23.7% compared with the control [33]. The bacterial communities
were shifted by the OLRs and micro-aeration. In addition, the
bacterial communities under micro-aeration conditions showed
higher abilities of hydrolysis, homoacetogenic acetate production
according to syntrophism.
The archaeal community structures of C1.1, M1.1, C1.5, M1.5, C2.1
and M2.1 at genus level are shown in Fig. 6b. Methanosaeta and
Methanobacterium were the most two dominant genera in all
collected samples. The relative abundances of Methanosaeta, a
specialist of exclusively using acetate as substrate to producing
methane [34], was at the dominant position in C1.1 and M1.1.
However, the archaea at the dominant position of relative abun-
dances in C1.5, M1.5, C2.1 and M2.1 were shifted to be Meth-
anobacterium, which is reported to be the hydrogenotrophic
archaea [35]. The relative abundances of Methanosaeta in M1.1,
M1.5 and M2.1 were 42.2%, 4.2% and 16.4%, which were 68.9%, 20.3%
and 57.0% of that in C1.1, C1.5, and C2.1, respectively. The results
indicated
that
micro-aeration
would
inhibit
the
growth
of
Methanosaeta. Similar results were also reported by a previous
study [14], who found the growth of Methanosaeta negatively
affected by the oxygen dosages, and its abundance was remarkable
lower at higher micro-aeration condition. The relative abundances
of Methanobacterium in M1.1, M1.5 and M2.1 were 35.2%, 81.4% and
66.4%, which were 56.9%, 33.3% and 14.3% higher than those of C1.1,
C1.5, and C2.1, respectively. Methanobacterium had higher abun-
dances in all micro-aerobic samples (M1.1, M1.5 and M2.1), sug-
gesting that hydrogenotrophic methanogens might possess a better
oxygen tolerance and ﬁnally become the dominant pathway to
produce methane under micro-aeration condition [14]. The anal-
ysis results mentioned above indicated that micro-aeration stim-
ulated the growth of Clostridia and Cloacimonadia to promote the
degradation of lignocellulosic biomass and VFAs syntrophic-
oxidization, providing more substrates for methanogens. At the
same time, oxygen-tolerant methanogens (e.g., Methanobacterium)
became the domain genera under micro-aerobic conditions, mak-
ing the methanogenesis on the rail.
3.6. Enzyme represented metabolic functions by PICRUSt
Hydrolysis is regarded as the rate-limiting step during AD of
cellulosic waste e.g., corn straw, and micro-aeration treatment has
been reported to be efﬁcient in accelerating the hydrolysis process
by stimulating the growth of facultative bacteria [5,14]. Biodegra-
dation of cellulose involves a series of extracellular cellulases e.g.,
endoglucanase (EC.3.2.1.4) and beta-glucosidase (EC.3.2.1.21) [36].
The relative abundances of critical enzymes related to the ligno-
cellulose degradation in C1.1, M1.1, C1.5, M1.5, C2.1 and M2.1 are
shown in Fig. 7. Endoglucanase and beta-glucosidase in M1.1, M1.5
and M2.1 possessed higher relative abundance than those in C1.1,
C1.5 and C2.1. Xylanase (EC 3.2.1.8) is an enzyme to degrade xylan,
which is the main content of hemicellulose in corn straw. The
relative abundance of xylanase in M1.1, M1.5 and M2.1 were all
higher compared with the control, especially in M1.5, which was
163% of C1.5. The higher cellulases and xylanase activity predicted
by PICRUSt in micro-aeration group indicated that micro-aeration
could stimulate the excretion of extracellular enzymes, thus
accelerate the degradation of lignocellulosic substrate, and beneﬁt
the methane production.
3.7. Effects of different concentration of SHAs on methanogenesis
Under micro-aeration conditions, the growth of facultative
bacteria was stimulated (Fig. 6a), more cellulase and xylanase were
excreted (Fig. 7), and SHAs concentrations were therefore higher
(Figs. 3 and 4). In order to investigate the effect of extracted SHAs

nogens e.g. Methanobacterium [43] and Methanosaeta [44] (Fig. 6b),
leading to higher methane production rate under micro-aerobic
conditions.
4. Conclusion
Micro-aeration led enhanced methane yield during semi-
continued AD of corn straw by regulation the microbial commu-
nity structures. Facultative bacteria that are capable of hydrolytic
enzyme secretion were stimulated by micro-aeration, leading to
faster hydrolysis and higher SHAs production. Meanwhile, metha-
nogens with a certain oxygen tolerance were enriched, making the
methanogenesis on the rail. In addition, the produced SHAs could
beneﬁt the syntrophic methanation by possibility acting as medi-
ator for DIET. The implementation of this study proved the bene-
ﬁcial effects of micro-aeration on the semi-continued AD of
cellulosic substrate, which could also provide references for the
industrial application of micro-aeration technology.
